title: Restrict Library Loading
summary: Programs rarely contain all of their code, so they load shared libraries, known as dynamic link libraries on Windows and shared objects on Linux, either at start up or on demand. Restricting library loading means controlling which of those files the operating system may bring into a process. The classic abuse path is search order hijacking, where an adversary places a file with a trusted name in a directory the loader checks before the legitimate one, so malicious code runs inside a signed process. Related behaviour includes injection into a running process and the use of preload environment variables on Linux. Defences include loading from absolute trusted paths, hardening the search order, validating signatures before load, restricting write access to program directories, and using platform features that allow only approved modules. Evidence of abuse includes unexpected modules in process listings, libraries loaded from temporary or user profile folders, unsigned modules inside signed processes, and file creation events in directories that should be read only.

beginner.definition: When a program starts, it often needs extra code files called libraries. On Windows these are dynamic link libraries, and on Linux they are shared objects. Restricting library loading means the system loads only library files that you trust. This stops an attacker from slipping their own file into a trusted program.
beginner.whyItMatters: A program trusts the libraries it loads, so a bad library runs with the same rights as the program itself. If that program is an admin tool or a backup service, the attacker gains those rights too. Attackers like this trick because it needs no memory exploit and often looks normal to monitoring tools. Weak folder permissions are usually the real problem behind it. Restricting loading closes that door and makes tampering easier to spot.
howItWorks: Programs ask the operating system to load libraries, and the system searches several folders.
The search order decides which matching file wins when the same name appears twice.
An attacker who can write to an early folder plants a file with a trusted name.
The program loads that file and runs the attacker's code inside itself.
You prevent this by loading from fixed trusted paths and hardening folder permissions.
You also check signatures and monitor which modules appear inside running processes.
beginner.example: Imagine a reading room where a runner fetches books for guests. The runner follows a fixed route and takes the first book with the right title, no matter who put it there. A prankster slips a fake book with the same title onto an early shelf. The runner picks it up and reads it aloud, so the room hears the prankster's words as if they were the author's. Signing every book and locking the early shelves fixes the problem. The reading room did nothing wrong, it simply trusted a shelf it did not control.
takeaways: A loaded library runs with the rights of the program that loads it.
Write permission on program folders is the root cause of most hijacking.
Watch module lists, because odd paths and unsigned files stand out.

objectives: Explain what a shared library is and why programs load them at runtime.
Describe how the library search order can be abused to run malicious code.
Identify folder permissions and configuration settings that reduce the risk.
Recognise evidence of suspicious module loading in process and file data.
Compare library loading restrictions on Windows and Linux in simple terms.
